title: Outcomes Over Outputs
editorial_note: Automated dialogue draft from the revised lesson. Review spoken wording and meaning before publishing.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Today we're talking about Outcomes Over Outputs. By the end, you'll know why this matters, how to use it, and what to notice in a real product.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: What is the problem we are trying to understand?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Outputs are features, screens, releases, and deliverables. Outcomes are changes in behaviour, capability, experience, or business value. Teams need outputs, but outcomes prevent shipping from becoming the definition of success.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: Why does that happen?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Frame outcomes around a person and an observable change. Then identify leading evidence, guardrails, and the assumptions connecting a solution to the outcome. A feature can launch perfectly and still fail to create value; an outcome lens creates permission to change or stop the feature when evidence demands it.

turns.speaker: host
turns.act: Write an outcome as observable change
turns.text: What changes when we look at write an outcome as observable change?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: The team builds a behaviour chain from comparison to informed selection, valid request, acknowledged review, appropriate appointment, and prepared attendance. Measures at each link diagnose failure, while guardrails cover safety, staff workload, access, and unresolved cases.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Shipping remains necessary, but it becomes one intervention whose contribution is tested rather than the definition of success.

turns.speaker: host
turns.act: Worked contrast: the metric can improve while the service worsens
turns.text: What changes when we look at worked contrast: the metric can improve while the service worsens?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Imagine the comparison doubles digital booking. A shallow outcome review declares success. A system review finds that the interface defaults to distant clinics with earlier dates, cancellation rises, staff manually correct unsuitable transfers, and patients without digital access wait longer because capacity moved.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: The output worked and the proxy improved; the intended outcome did not.

turns.speaker: host
turns.act: Write an outcome with a causal model
turns.text: What changes when we look at write an outcome with a causal model?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Specify whose state or behaviour should change, from what baseline, in which context, by when, and why that represents value. Separate customer outcome, business outcome, product behaviour, and team output. “Launch recommendations” is output; “people make a confident suitable choice” is closer to outcome.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Map assumptions from intervention to behaviour and result. Add guardrails for trust, accessibility, safety, cost, and unintended work. Choose leading evidence without allowing an easy proxy to replace the desired change.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Review outcomes through segments and longer horizons. A local conversion gain may conflict with retention or staff burden. Outcome orientation is not metric obedience; it is explicit reasoning about value and consequence.

turns.speaker: host
turns.act: Build a behaviour chain to the outcome
turns.text: What changes when we look at build a behaviour chain to the outcome?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Measures distinguish leading behaviour, service outcome, and longer-term value. Guardrails cover safety, original-appointment loss, unequal delay, staff workload, and support. If request submission rises while suitable appointments do not, the team investigates the broken link rather than declaring success.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Outcome language also clarifies ownership. Product teams can influence comprehension and request quality; clinics and operations control other parts. A whole-service owner coordinates the shared result so internal boundaries do not shrink the customer promise.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: Where does the harder design decision appear?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Outcome framing exposes conflicting incentives. A short-term engagement lift may damage trust or completion quality. Define the user benefit and guardrails before optimising the visible number.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: What should we look at more closely?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: An outcome has a subject, a change, a context, and a reason it matters. “Improve activation” is too broad until the team can say which people should reach which meaningful behaviour, under what conditions, and why that signifies value.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Connect outcome measures to a theory of change: the opportunity addressed, the intervention, the expected mechanism, and possible negative effects. This makes it possible to learn when the mechanism fails rather than simply declaring a feature unsuccessful.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Use a balanced measure set. Leading indicators help teams see whether a path is forming; outcome measures show whether value persists; guardrails reveal harm, exclusion, support burden, privacy cost, or declining trust. Avoid using a metric as a target without inspecting what behaviour it incentivises.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: An outcome is not merely a business number; it should represent a better state for the people and system involved.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Failure modes to watch

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Output theatre: releases are celebrated while their intended change is never measured. Metric proxy: a convenient count replaces the value it was meant to represent. No guardrails: a local improvement hides harm or workload shifted elsewhere. Frozen outcome: a goal remains relevant only to an old strategy or context.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: Can we see that in a concrete product situation?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Releasing reminders is an output. Fewer missed appointments may be an outcome, but only if reminders reach people, are understood, and do not increase privacy harm or cancellation barriers.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: How does this connect to what we have already learned?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Discovery is a habit because outcomes must be revisited. lesson 27 teaches how recurring conversations reveal the past behaviour behind those outcomes.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: What should I notice the next time I use a product?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Convert “launch feature X” into a measurable user outcome. What behaviour would show it worked?
